The Plateau pika (Ochotona curzoniae) displays a resting metabolic rate that has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted at the species' typical active body temperature. Under thermal conditions of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], field-caught individuals exhibited a basal oxygen consumption of 218 milliliters per hour [JOi = 218 milliliters per hour], a value that positions this lagomorph at the higher end of the metabolic spectrum for its body size. Neonates are born weighing 9 grams [Wwb = 9 grams], a modest birth mass that is comparable to estimates derived from the closely related American pika, Ochotona princeps, upon which part of this measurement is based. This initial mass is remarkably low relative to the ultimate adult body mass, which reaches 218 grams [Wwi = 218 grams] in fully grown individuals, representing a roughly twenty-four-fold increase from the newborn stage.

Reproductive output in Plateau pika populations has been characterized through long-term field surveys on the Tibetan Plateau. Females typically produce 1 to 2 litters annually [F_R_i = 1 to 2 litters annually], with each litter containing between 1 and 8 pups [N_R_i = each litter containing between 1 and 8 pups], though the mean litter size has been reported at 4.8 pups. At the species' normothermic body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], a female achieving the upper bounds of both litter size and frequency yields a maximum annual reproductive output of up to 16 pups per year. Such fecundity is notable for a small mammal inhabiting a high-altitude environment where growing seasons are compressed and resource availability fluctuates considerably across the short alpine summer.

The developmental chronology of the Plateau pika unfolds within a relatively compressed timeframe, a necessity given the brief productive period of its alpine meadow habitat. Following a gestation period that spans 22 days [tg = 22 days] at the species' normothermic body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], which is consistent with the 21 to 24 day range documented in earlier studies, altricial neonates are born. These newborn pups weigh approximately 9 grams [Wwb = approximately 9 grams] and depend entirely on maternal milk for their early growth. The time from birth to weaning is 21 days [tx = 21 days], a relatively brief nursing period that contrasts with the 8 to 9 week weaning age observed in some other ochotonids, underscoring the accelerated pace of early life development in this species at a temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C].

Juveniles that successfully transition to nutritional independence at weaning, when they reach approximately 63 grams [Wwx = approximately 63 grams] in wet weight, enter a rapid growth phase as they approach maturity. This weaning mass of 63 grams [Wwx = 63 grams] represents a sevenfold increase over the 9 grams recorded at birth, reflecting the efficiency of maternal milk provisioning. The interval between birth and the attainment of puberty spans 300 days [tp = 300 days] when measured at the body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], meaning that individuals born early in one breeding season typically do not reach sexual maturity until the following year. This 10-month pre-reproductive period is a substantial commitment for a small lagomorph, though it aligns with the seasonal constraints imposed by the harsh Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau environment.

Longevity records for the Plateau pika indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years] under field conditions at a body temperature of 40.1 °C [T = 40.1 °C], a relatively modest duration that reflects the high predation pressure and energetic demands of alpine life. Adult asymptotic body mass of approximately 218 grams [Wwi = approximately 218 grams] is attained well within the first year, long before senescence sets in. A female producing 1 to 2 litters annually [F_R_i = 1 to 2 litters annually] and averaging 4.8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.8 pups per litter] can contribute substantially to population turnover, with the combination of a 63 gram weaning mass, a 9 gram birth weight, and a 22 day gestation period collectively enabling a fast-paced life history strategy adapted to one of the world's most challenging terrestrial ecosystems.
